newsitem.title: USA: Damage to copper market done - Deutsche Sharp.
newsitem.headline: Damage to copper market done - Deutsche Sharp.

text.p: The damage to the world's copper market, done by the Sumitomo affair earlier this year, is now largely over, with good economic indicators pointing towards healthy growth in demand, said Richard Hirsch of Deutsche Sharps Pixley Metals Inc.
"Most of the damage on the price charts has now been done," Hirsch told the Copper Roundtable at the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries (ISRI) conference in Chicago Wednesday.
"There is value in copper at 90 cents a lb and I would buy at 88 cents a lb - but given the recent price range, I am a happier buyer at 88 cents than 91 cents," he added.
Currently there was a mismatch between the price and inventories which were sufficient for only four weeks consumption, Hirsch said.
"Economic indicators for leading industrialized countries point to good growth in copper consumption, estimated conservatively at 1.5 percent per year," he said.
But a "tsunami" of mine supplies is probably coming and that may be the reason why the market is down to 90 cents a lb, he said.
Hirsch cautioned that some new mining projects may be delayed or cancelled and noted that few mines, if any, were hedged as far forward as 1999.
Although the indications were that industrial production and copper demand globally was about to turn up, the momentum on the downside in base metals prices was still there, he said.
"There was usually a six to nine month gap between an upturn in industrial indicators and the resulting feed-through into consumption," he said.
"Copper has been cleared out - most of the aggressive selling is out of the market, he said.
"Most of the producers have closed out most of their options and that allows the banks to close out their risks," he said.
"Most of the shorts have taken their profits but not all," he said.
